query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: The structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications is governed by the configurational entropy and the resulting formation of a single-phase solid solution, which leads to enhanced mechanical properties such as high hardness, strength, and softening resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy nanoalloys with a single-phase solid solution structure
generation.structural_mediator: Configurational entropy and the formation of a single-phase solid solution
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy of high-entropy nanoalloys leads to the formation of a single-phase solid solution, which in turn enhances the mechanical properties of the alloy by reducing the formation of intermetallic compounds and promoting a more homogeneous microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced structural and chemical stability, as well as improved mechanical properties such as high hardness, strength, and softening resistance, compared to traditional alloys.
generation.baseline: Traditional alloys with lower configurational entropy and a more complex microstructure
generation.boundary: The prediction is limited to high-entropy nanoalloys with a single-phase solid solution structure and may not apply to alloys with a more complex microstructure or those that undergo significant phase transformations at high temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between configurational entropy and the resulting mechanical properties is still not fully understood and requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: A comparative study of the mechanical properties of high-entropy nanoalloys with different configurational entropies, subjected to high-temperature applications.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy nanoalloys with higher configurational entropy do not exhibit enhanced mechanical properties compared to those with lower configurational entropy, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).

High entropy or multi principal element alloys are a promising and relatively young concept for designing alloys. The idea of creating alloys without a single main alloying element opens up a wide space for possible new alloy compositions. High entropy alloys based on refractory metals such as W, Mo, Ta or Nb are of interest for future high temperature applications e.g., in the aerospace or chemical industry. However, producing refractory metal high entropy alloys by conventional metallurgical methods remains challenging. For this reason, the feasibility of laser-based additive manufacturing of the refractory metal high entropy alloy W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 by laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) is investigated in the present work. In-situ alloy formation from mixtures of easily available elemental powders is employed to avoid an expensive atomization of pre-alloyed powder. It is shown that PBF-LB/M of W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 is in general possible and that a complete fusion of the powder mixture without a significant number of undissolved particles is achievable by in-situ alloy formation during PBF-LB/M when selecting favorable process parameter combinations. Abstract Developing affordable and light high-temperature materials alternative to Ni-base superalloys has significantly increased the efforts in designing advanced ferritic superalloys. However, currently developed ferritic superalloys still exhibit low high-temperature strengths, which limits their usage. Here we use a CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational method to design light, strong, and low-cost high-entropy alloys for elevated-temperature applications. Through the high-throughput screening, precipitation-strengthened lightweight high-entropy alloys are discovered from thousands of initial compositions, which exhibit enhanced strengths compared to other counterparts at room and elevated temperatures. The experimental and theoretical understanding of both successful and failed cases in their strengthening mechanisms and order-disorder transitions further improves the accuracy of the thermodynamic database of the discovered alloy system. decision.trend: The trend in the research on high-entropy alloys is towards understanding their structural and chemical stability under various conditions, including high-temperature applications and irradiation. Earlier studies focused on the effects of composition and processing on the microstructure and properties of these alloys. More recent studies have investigated the deformation mechanisms, creep behavior, and radiation resistance of high-entropy alloys. The use of advanced characterization techniques, such as in situ TEM and neutron diffraction, has provided valuable insights into the behavior of these alloys at the atomic scale.
decision.unsolved: One of the remaining unsolved questions in the field of high-entropy alloys is the understanding of the governing factors that control their structural and chemical stability in high-temperature applications. While significant progress has been made in understanding the effects of composition and processing on the properties of these alloys, the underlying mechanisms that govern their stability under extreme conditions are not yet fully understood.
